title: Bandola (Andean plectrum lute)
summary: The bandola is a pear-shaped plucked lute of the Colombian Andes. It has a flat back, several courses of strings, and is played with a plectrum whose quick repeated strokes make a rolling tremolo. It carries the tune in dance bands and songs.
howToPlay: Four courses of strings run down the neck, the lowest on the left. Each lane marks the fret where a note is played.
A bead slides down the strings to its fret. Strike the lane as the bead lands.
The long lane over the strings is the tremolo: tap it on the beat and the note rolls on its own.
Try the pasillo line first, then the tremolo song, then the quick scale.
rules: The notes come from a scale starting on A, with a high pair of notes on the top course.
The tremolo lane sounds a rolled note and is scored once, at its start.
A stroke on the beat is perfect, a near one is good, and extra strokes cost points.
The pasillo line counts three beats to the bar; the quick scale counts two; the others four.
heritageNote: The bandola has been the singing voice of Andean string bands in Colombia for generations. Makers carve and join the pale pear-shaped body from several woods, and players keep their plectrum strokes quick and even.
